chapter.name: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

questions.q: In the Grade 8 Curiosity book, a kite is drawn in the top corner of every right-hand page. What does the book say this kite stands for?
questions.a: Curiosity must take flight if we are to explore the unknown.
o: Curiosity must take flight if we are to explore the unknown.
A deep, solid foundation of knowledge linked to our heritage.
Hidden scientific thoughts that make the page less boring.
The motion of objects in the sky that gave us calendars.

questions.q: The book reminds students what each earlier grade taught about science. Which idea does it say was learnt in Grade 7?
questions.a: Science is always evolving, and each answer opens new questions.
o: Science is always evolving, and each answer opens new questions.
Science begins with wonder and simple 'Why?' and 'How?' questions.
Science means designing simple experiments to answer focused questions.
Science is a fixed set of facts that are learnt once and kept.

questions.q: True or False? 'The book says it wants students not only to learn new facts, but to learn how to find new facts.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The book says it does not want students just to learn new facts but to learn how to find them: by asking focused questions, doing simple experiments and using their observations to improve their understanding.
s: States True
Explains that finding facts means asking focused questions, experimenting and using observations

questions.q: (a) What does the image of a root at the bottom of the left-hand pages of the book symbolise? (b) Name one thing the book says this foundation keeps us connected to.
questions.a: (a) A deep, solid foundation of knowledge. (b) Any one of: our environment, our traditions, our cultural and natural heritage.
s: (a) A deep, solid foundation of knowledge
(b) Names the environment, traditions, or cultural and natural heritage

questions.q: The book says investigation in science means more than just looking at something and asking only simple questions. Write the three things it says a Grade 8 student can now do.
questions.a: (1) Ask more focused questions. (2) Design ways to do simple experiments to answer those questions. (3) Use the observations to improve her understanding.
s: Asks more focused questions
Designs simple experiments to answer them
Uses observations to improve understanding

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A student who only memorises the facts printed in this book has not yet done what the book means by investigation.
Reason (R): The book says it wants students to learn how to find new facts, not just to learn new facts.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read these statements about the opening pages of the Grade 8 book.
I. The book's examples of puzzles to investigate range from an everyday one, why dough rises, to a bigger mystery, whether the world is getting warmer.
II. The patterns in the lines at the bottom of the pages hide some scientific thoughts, but they are there mainly to make the page less boring.
III. The kite on the right-hand pages stands for the solid foundation of knowledge that connects us to our heritage.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: True or False? 'In Grade 8 the book leaves behind the wonder of Grade 6 and the evolving ideas of Grade 7, and replaces them with investigation.' Give the verdict and the correct idea.
questions.a: False. The book says that in Grade 8, wonder and evolution come together to form the heart of how science works. Investigation builds on them; it does not replace them.
s: States False
Says wonder and evolution come together in Grade 8 and investigation builds on them

questions.q: Three friends in Kolhapur plan a weekend project on the book's question 'Why does dough rise?'. Plan X (Sneha): read three websites and copy out what they say. Plan Y (Omkar): imagine five possible reasons and write a story about each, without testing any of them. Plan Z (Pallavi): keep two bowls of the same dough, one in a warm corner and one in a cool corner, note how each looks every 30 minutes, then suggest a reason and plan a test of it. Using the book's root and kite symbols and its idea of investigation, judge each plan and say which one is closest to what the book wants.
questions.a: Plan X only gathers facts others have found; it has neither careful observation of her own nor creative ideas, so it is learning facts, not finding them. Plan Y has the kite (ideas that soar) but no root, since it is not grounded in any real observation. Plan Z uses careful observation (the root) and then a creative idea to test (the kite). Plan Z is closest, because the book says investigation works best when careful observation is balanced with creative thinking.
s: Judges Plan X: copying facts is not finding facts
Judges Plan Y: ideas without real observation (kite without root)
Judges Plan Z: observation plus an idea to test (root and kite)
Chooses Plan Z, citing the balance of observation and creative thinking

questions.q:
Diya, a Class 8 student in Mangaluru, wrote these entries in her science diary about the bathroom mirror.
(a) 'Why does the mirror fog up after a hot bath?'
(b) 'I used to think the fog was smoke. When I wiped it, my fingers got wet, so now I think it is water, and that makes me ask where the water comes from.'
(c) 'I took baths of 2, 5 and 10 minutes with the same hot water and noted how many minutes the fog took to clear each time.'
(d) 'My cousin told me the answer, so I wrote it down and stopped.'
For each of (a) to (d), say which way of doing science from the book it shows best: Grade 6 wonder, Grade 7 evolving ideas, Grade 8 investigation, or only learning a fact. Then (e) rewrite entry (a) as a focused question that she could investigate.
questions.a: (a) Grade 6 wonder: a simple 'Why?' question. (b) Grade 7 evolving ideas: her idea changed after a new observation, and the answer opened a new question. (c) Grade 8 investigation: a focused question tested by changing one thing (the bath time) and recording observations. (d) Only learning a fact: she received an answer but did not find it out herself. (e) For example: 'Does a longer hot bath make the mirror take longer to clear?'
s: (a) Grade 6 wonder, a simple why question
(b) Grade 7: idea changed and opened a new question
(c) Grade 8 investigation: one thing changed, observations recorded
(d) Only learning a fact, not finding it
(e) A focused question naming what is changed and what is observed

questions.q: According to the book's preview, which effect of electric current helps motors run and machines function?
questions.a: The magnetic effect
o: The magnetic effect
The heating effect
The effect of a pressure difference
The reflection of light

questions.q: Which of these is NOT given in the book's preview as something that helps us stay healthy and fight infections?
questions.a: Keeping away from every microbe
o: Keeping away from every microbe
Eating nutritious food
Doing regular exercise
Taking vaccines and medicines

questions.q: (a) What are microbes, as the book's preview describes them? (b) Give one way in which some microbes help us.
questions.a: (a) Microbes are tiny organisms, such as those found in a single drop of water, that we cannot see but that are deeply linked to us. (b) Some help us digest our food, or help produce medicines.
s: (a) Tiny organisms, unseen but linked to us
(b) Help digest food or produce medicines

questions.q: (a) The book says it will study forces, starting with those that change how objects move. Name the three changes in motion it lists. (b) Which of these changes happens when a car's brakes are applied?
questions.a: (a) Forces can make objects speed up, slow down or change direction. (b) The car slows down (until it stops).
s: (a) Speed up, slow down, change direction
(b) Slow down

questions.q: Answer in one line each, from the book's preview. (a) What can harmful microbes cause? (b) Which effect of electric current do we depend on to keep us warm? (c) A ball thrown up in the air falls back to the ground. Which topic does the book say helps explain this?
questions.a: (a) Infections. (b) The heating effect. (c) Forces.
s: (a) Infections
(b) The heating effect
(c) Forces

questions.q:
Use the ideas in the book's preview to say what each of these shows: the heating effect of electric current, the magnetic effect of electric current, a helpful microbe, a harmful microbe, or a force changing motion.
(a) An electric blanket keeps a patient warm on a cold night in Srinagar.
(b) The motor of a mixer-grinder turns its blades.
(c) Tiny organisms in our body help us digest the food we eat.
(d) A scraped knee becomes infected by tiny organisms.
(e) A goalkeeper's hands stop a football that was rolling towards the goal.
questions.a: (a) The heating effect of electric current. (b) The magnetic effect of electric current (it helps motors run). (c) A helpful microbe. (d) A harmful microbe (causing an infection). (e) A force making the ball slow down and stop.
s: (a) Heating effect
(b) Magnetic effect
(c) Helpful microbe
(d) Harmful microbe
(e) A force slowing the ball down

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Some microbes are helpful to us.
Reason (R): Some microbes are harmful and cause infections.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Each question in Column I belongs to one stop on the book's journey in Column II. Match them.
Column I: I. Why does my phone charger get warm while it is working?  II. Why does a rolling marble come to a stop on a carpet?  III. What lives in a single drop of pond water?  IV. How does a vaccine protect a child before she falls ill?
Column II: A. Microbes  B. Staying healthy and fighting infections  C. Effects of electric current  D. Forces
questions.a: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B
o: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B
I-D, II-C, III-A, IV-B
I-C, II-D, III-B, IV-A
I-C, II-A, III-D, IV-B

questions.q: A school bus in Ranchi starts from rest at the school gate, moves along a straight road, turns left at a crossing and finally stops at the next bus stop. Name two different moments in this trip when a force changes the bus's motion, and say which kind of change the force causes each time.
questions.a: Any two of: starting from the gate, a force makes the bus speed up; turning left at the crossing, a force makes it change direction; stopping at the bus stop, a force makes it slow down and stop.
s: First moment with the correct change (speed up, change direction or slow down)
A second, different moment with its correct change

questions.q:
A small tailoring unit in Tiruppur has 2 electric sewing machines, each run by a motor, and 2 electric irons, each with a coil that gets hot. Today 40 shirts must be stitched and then ironed; a shirt can be ironed only after it is stitched. One machine stitches 10 shirts an hour and one iron presses 20 shirts an hour. There is a 3-hour power cut, and the backup inverter can run only 2 of the 4 appliances at a time.
(a) Which effect of electric current does a sewing machine's motor use?
(b) Which effect of electric current does an electric iron use?
(c) Plan A runs one machine and one iron together for all 3 hours. How many shirts are stitched by the end?
(d) Plan B runs both machines for the first 2 hours and then both irons for the last hour. Which plan gets all 40 shirts stitched and ironed? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) The magnetic effect (it helps motors run). (b) The heating effect. (c) 1 machine x 10 shirts an hour x 3 hours = 30 shirts, so 10 shirts are left unstitched. (d) Plan B: 2 machines x 10 x 2 hours = 40 shirts stitched, then 2 irons x 20 x 1 hour = 40 shirts ironed, all within 3 hours. Plan A fails because only 30 shirts are stitched, so Plan B should be chosen.
s: (a) Magnetic effect
(b) Heating effect
(c) 30 shirts stitched under Plan A
(d) Shows Plan B gives 40 stitched in 2 h and 40 ironed in 1 h, and chooses Plan B

questions.q: How does the book's preview describe a compound?
questions.a: Two or more elements bonded together
o: Two or more elements bonded together
A pure substance made of a single element
A combination that can be separated physically
Sugar that has dissolved in tea

questions.q: According to the book, what usually results in a gentle breeze?
questions.a: A small difference in air pressure
o: A small difference in air pressure
A strong difference in air pressure
Air particles that cannot move at all
Light bending as it passes through air

questions.q:
Match each word in Column I with the book's description or example of it in Column II.
Column I: I. Element  II. Compound  III. Mixture  IV. Solution
Column II: A. A combination that can be separated physically  B. A pure substance  C. Sugar dissolved in tea to make it sweet  D. Two or more elements bonded together
questions.a: I-B, II-D, III-A, IV-C
o: I-B, II-D, III-A, IV-C
I-D, II-B, III-A, IV-C
I-B, II-A, III-D, IV-C
I-B, II-D, III-C, IV-A

questions.q: Using the book's preview of particles: (a) How much can the particles of a solid brick move? (b) How do the particles of the air inside a football move?
questions.a: (a) The particles of a solid such as a brick cannot move much. (b) Air is a gas, so its particles can move around freely.
s: (a) Solid particles cannot move much
(b) Gas particles move around freely

questions.q: Answer from the book's preview. (a) What is pressure? (b) Name one powerful weather event that a strong pressure difference can lead to. (c) Name two parts of our lives that the book says such weather events affect.
questions.a: (a) Pressure is how a force is distributed over an object. (b) Strong winds, storms or cyclones (any one). (c) Any two of: our daily lives, agriculture, our safety.
s: (a) How force is distributed over an object
(b) Cyclones, storms or strong winds
(c) Two of daily life, agriculture, safety

questions.q:
Read these statements from a student's summary of the book's preview of matter.
I. The book calls classifying things around us an important feature of science.
II. The book describes a mixture as two or more elements bonded together.
III. The book says that in solids, particles can move around freely.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only
o: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A gentle breeze is caused by a large difference in air pressure.
Reason (R): The book says that the same ideas of force and pressure decide how air moves.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: Meera writes in her notebook: 'Everything around us is made of tiny particles. In solids the particles cannot move at all, and in gases they cannot move much.' Check each part of her note against the book's preview and correct whatever is wrong.
questions.a: Part 1 is correct: the book says everything around us is made of tiny particles. Part 2 is wrong: the book says particles in a solid cannot move much, not that they cannot move at all. Part 3 is wrong: in gases the particles can move around freely.
s: Accepts that everything is made of tiny particles
Corrects solids: particles cannot move much (not 'not at all')
Corrects gases: particles move around freely

questions.q: Sample P is made of two elements bonded together. Sample Q is some of Sample P stirred together with sand, and the sand can be picked out again by sieving. Using the book's definitions, which statement is correct?
questions.a: P is a compound and Q is a mixture.
o: P is a compound and Q is a mixture.
P is a mixture and Q is a compound.
Both are compounds, since both contain more than one element.
Both are mixtures, since both contain more than one substance.

questions.q:
A science teacher in Raipur gives two groups the same four sample cards. Card K: 'made of only one element, carbon'. Card L: 'carbon and oxygen bonded together'. Card M: 'sand and salt grains stirred together; they can be separated by physical means'. Card N: 'iron and sulphur bonded together'. Each group sorts the cards into Element, Compound or Mixture. A correct card earns 5 points and a wrong card loses 2 points. Group 1 sorted: K element, L mixture, M mixture, N compound. Group 2 sorted: K compound, L compound, M compound, N compound.
(a) Which cards are compounds, by the book's definition?
(b) Which card is the element, and why?
(c) Find the score of each group.
(d) Which group better understood the difference between a compound and a mixture? Justify using their answers.
questions.a: (a) Cards L and N, because each has two elements bonded together. (b) Card K, because it is a pure substance made of only one element. (c) Group 1: K, M and N correct, L wrong, so 3 x 5 - 2 = 13 points. Group 2: L and N correct, K and M wrong, so 2 x 5 - 2 x 2 = 6 points. (d) Group 1: it sorted the mixture M and the compound N correctly and lost marks only on L, while Group 2 called everything a compound, even M, which can be separated physically and is therefore a mixture. Group 1's higher score (13 against 6) agrees.
s: (a) L and N, elements bonded together
(b) K, a pure substance of one element
(c) Group 1 = 13 and Group 2 = 6
(d) Chooses Group 1, noting Group 2 called the physically separable M a compound

questions.q: According to the book's preview, watching which of these allowed humans to come up with the first calendars?
questions.a: The periodic cycles of the Moon's phases
o: The periodic cycles of the Moon's phases
Light bending as it passes through lenses
The pressure differences that cause winds
The way particles move around in gases

questions.q: The book says Earth's atmosphere helps make Earth 'just right' for life. Which pair of jobs does it give the atmosphere?
questions.a: It provides the oxygen we breathe and shields us from harmful ultraviolet rays.
o: It provides the oxygen we breathe and shields us from harmful ultraviolet rays.
It keeps Earth at the right distance from the Sun and lights up the Moon.
It makes the phases of the Moon and fixes the dates of our calendars.
It provides the oxygen we breathe and keeps Earth's temperature from ever changing.

questions.q: True or False? 'The Moon shows phases because it makes its own light, and this light grows and shrinks from night to night.' Give the verdict and the correct idea.
questions.a: False. The Moon reflects light; it does not make its own. Depending on the relative positions of the Earth, Moon and Sun, a slightly different part of the Moon is lit each night, which gives the phases.
s: States False
Says the Moon reflects light and a different part is lit each night because of the positions of Earth, Moon and Sun

questions.q: (a) What does the book mean by an ecosystem? (b) Name two things from the book that every living being depends on and responds to.
questions.a: (a) An ecosystem is formed by the patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environment (and each other) that support life. (b) Any two of: air, water, sunlight, other organisms around them.
s: (a) Relationships between living organisms and their environment
(b) Any two of air, water, sunlight, other organisms

questions.q: Answer from the book's preview of light. (a) What happens to light when it passes through a lens? (b) Name the two kinds of mirror that the book says light rays reflect off. (c) Name one way in which this study of light helps many people in daily life.
questions.a: (a) It bends. (b) Flat mirrors and curved mirrors. (c) Corrective glasses help many of us see clearly.
s: (a) Light bends
(b) Flat and curved mirrors
(c) Corrective glasses help people see clearly

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A rough surface, such as a sheet of plain cardboard, reflects light.
Reason (R): Only polished surfaces that show a clear image can reflect light.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the idea from the book's preview that fits it in Column II.
Column I: I. A family fixes its festival dates by counting new Moons and full Moons.  II. The curved side mirror of a scooter shows the road behind.  III. Owls, mice and grass in a field depend on one another.  IV. A layer of air around Earth keeps harmful ultraviolet rays away.
Column II: A. Light reflecting off a curved mirror  B. Earth's atmosphere  C. Calendars built from the Moon's phases  D. An ecosystem
questions.a: I-C, II-A, III-D, IV-B
o: I-C, II-A, III-D, IV-B
I-A, II-C, III-D, IV-B
I-C, II-A, III-B, IV-D
I-D, II-A, III-C, IV-B

questions.q: In a quiz, Tanya is asked: 'Which of these living beings does not depend on or respond to the air, water, sunlight or other organisms around it?' The choices are a whale in the deep sea, a blade of grass and a tiny insect. Which answer fits the book's description of ecosystems?
questions.a: None of them; all living beings depend on these.
o: None of them; all living beings depend on these.
The whale, since it lives deep in the sea, far from sunlight.
The blade of grass, since it does not depend on other organisms.
The tiny insect, since it is too small to need much air or water.

questions.q: The book says the first calendars came from watching the Moon's phases, but that various calendars came into being by combining careful observations of sunrises, sunsets and lunar cycles. Explain why a calendar maker needs both kinds of observation, and what each one gives the calendar.
questions.a: The Moon's phases repeat in a periodic cycle, so they give a longer repeating period of time (from one phase back to the same phase). Sunrises and sunsets mark each day, so they let the maker count the days within each cycle. Combining the two, as the book says, gives a calendar that fixes our daily routines from the motions of the Sun and Moon.
s: The repeating cycle of the Moon's phases gives a longer repeating period
Sunrises and sunsets mark days, so days can be counted within the cycle
Concludes that combining both gives a working calendar, as the book says

questions.q: 'Earth is just right for life, but we can upset this balance, and we can also help protect it.' Justify this statement in five points, using only what the book's preview says about Earth's distance from the Sun, its atmosphere, human activities and the role of science.
questions.a: (1) Earth lies at the right distance from the Sun for water to remain liquid. (2) Its atmosphere provides the oxygen we breathe. (3) The atmosphere also shields us from harmful ultraviolet rays. (4) Human activities can cause small changes in Earth's temperature that disrupt climate patterns, with dangerous consequences, so we can upset the balance. (5) We can also use science, observing, measuring and experimenting, to understand these changes and guide our actions, so we can help protect it.
s: Distance from the Sun keeps water liquid
Atmosphere provides oxygen
Atmosphere shields from harmful ultraviolet rays
Human activities cause small temperature changes that disrupt climate
Science (observing, measuring, experimenting) can guide our actions

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter list as something we can control when we fry a puri?
questions.a: The temperature of the hot oil
o: The temperature of the hot oil
The time the puri takes to puff up
Whether the puri puffs up or not
Whether one side of the puri turns out thinner

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter mean by something we can 'change or control' in an experiment? (b) Give two examples of such things from the chapter's puri investigation.
questions.a: (a) It is something the investigator decides and sets herself when doing the experiment, to see whether changing it makes a difference to what she observes. (b) Any two of: the thickness of the rolled dough, the size of the rolled dough, the type of flour (atta, maida), the temperature of the oil, the way the dough is dropped into the oil.
s: (a) Something the investigator sets or changes herself during the experiment
(b) Any two of thickness, size, flour type, oil temperature, way of dropping

questions.q: The chapter says you do not need a fancy laboratory, because even your kitchen is a wonderful place to do science. (a) Name the three things it says you need to start with. (b) Name one food other than a puri that the chapter describes puffing up or swelling.
questions.a: (a) Curiosity, careful observation, and asking 'what happens if...?'. (b) A batura (puffs up in hot oil) or a phulka (swells when put directly on the flame).
s: (a) Curiosity, careful observation, asking what happens if
(b) Batura or phulka

questions.q: Apart from the type of flour, write three different things from the chapter's list that we can control when making and frying a puri.
questions.a: Any three of: the thickness of the rolled dough; the size of the rolled dough; the temperature of the hot oil; the way the rolled dough is put into the oil (dropped vertically, slid at an angle, slid slowly).
s: First correct controllable thing
Second, different controllable thing
Third, different controllable thing

questions.q:
Meenu's family in Kanpur makes puris every Sunday. This Sunday she wants to investigate them like a scientist. In the kitchen she finds a packet of atta and a packet of maida, a rolling pin, a kadhai of oil on a stove whose knob can be turned to a high or a low flame, and her mother's kitchen timer that counts seconds. She writes her scientific question: 'What are the different things that may change the way a puri puffs up?'
(a) Name one thing she can control using the two packets.
(b) Name one thing she can control using the stove knob.
(c) Name one thing she can control using the rolling pin.
(d) Name one thing she can measure using the timer.
questions.a: (a) The type of flour (atta or maida). (b) The temperature of the oil. (c) The thickness (or the size) of the rolled dough. (d) The time, in seconds, that a puri takes to puff up.
s: (a) Type of flour
(b) Oil temperature
(c) Thickness or size of the dough
(d) Time taken to puff up, in seconds

questions.q: Shreya uses the chapter's way of planning to investigate how a papad curls when it is roasted over a gas flame. Which of these is something she controls, not something she observes?
questions.a: How high above the flame she holds the papad
o: How high above the flame she holds the papad
Whether the papad curls up at the edges
How many seconds the papad takes to curl
Whether brown spots appear on the papad's surface

questions.q:
Read these statements about the chapter's puri investigation.
I. The chapter's scientific question asks what different things may change the way a puri puffs up when fried.
II. The chapter lists the thickness of the rolled dough as something we observe, not something we control.
III. Sliding the rolled dough slowly into the oil is one of the ways the chapter suggests for putting it in.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: True or False? 'In the chapter's puri investigation, the way the rolled dough is put into the oil is something we can control.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The investigator decides whether to drop the dough vertically, slide it at an angle or slide it slowly, so it is set by her; the chapter lists it among the things we can control.
s: States True
Explains that she chooses how the dough goes in (vertically, at an angle, slowly), as the chapter lists

questions.q: Ayaan wants to take the book's everyday puzzle 'Why does dough rise?' and plan an investigation of it, the way the chapter plans the puri investigation. (a) Write his scientific question in the same form as the chapter's puri question. (b) Name two things he could control. (c) Name one observation with a yes/no answer and one he could measure as a number. (d) Explain why the chapter's method needs him to sort his list into these two groups before he starts.
questions.a: (a) For example: 'What are the different things that may change how much a dough rises?' (b) Any two sensible controllable things, for example the type of flour, the amount of water mixed in, or how warm the place where the dough is kept. (c) Yes/no: did the dough rise? Number: for example the height the dough reaches in centimetres, or the time it takes to rise, in minutes. (d) The chapter says we must find out what we can change or control and what we can observe; only then can we change a controlled thing and see from the observations whether it made any difference.
s: (a) A question in the form 'what things may change how the dough rises'
(b) Two things he sets himself
(c) One yes/no and one measurable observation
(d) Controlled things are changed and observations show whether the change made a difference

questions.q: Lakshmi's list for a puri investigation reads: 1. type of flour; 2. time taken to puff up; 3. temperature of the oil; 4. whether one side is thinner; 5. size of the dough circle; 6. whether the puri puffs up. (a) Sort the list into things she controls and things she observes. (b) Which item on the list gives a number that she can measure?
questions.a: (a) Controls: 1 (type of flour), 3 (temperature of the oil) and 5 (size of the dough circle). Observes: 2 (time taken to puff up), 4 (whether one side is thinner) and 6 (whether it puffs up). (b) Item 2, the time taken to puff up, measured in seconds.
s: (a) Controls 1, 3, 5 and observes 2, 4, 6
(b) Item 2, time to puff in seconds

questions.q: In the chapter's puri investigation, which observation gives a number that we can measure?
questions.a: The time the puri takes to puff up, in seconds
o: The time the puri takes to puff up, in seconds
Whether or not the puri puffs up in the oil
The type of flour used to make the dough
Whether the oil smoked while frying the puri

questions.q: (a) What name does the chapter give to the way all scientific experiments, from the simple to the most complicated, are done? (b) Give one habit from the chapter that is part of it.
questions.a: (a) Systematic investigation. (b) Any one of: changing only one thing at a time while keeping the other conditions the same; keeping notes of everything seen and sensed; observing or measuring the result carefully; asking new questions after a round of experiments.
s: (a) Systematic investigation
(b) One correct habit, such as changing one thing at a time or keeping notes

questions.q: Answer from the chapter in one line each. (a) Name one thing about the oil that the chapter says is worth noting during a puri experiment. (b) Write one new question that the chapter says may come up after one round of puri experiments. (c) Do scientists today completely understand why a puri puffs up?
questions.a: (a) Whether the oil splattered, smelled or smoked (any one). (b) Do puris puff better when made fresh or from stored dough? or What happens if I prick a hole in the puri before frying? (c) No, the chapter says even this is not completely understood by scientists today.
s: (a) Splatter, smell or smoke
(b) Fresh versus stored dough, or pricking a hole
(c) No, it is not completely understood

questions.q: The chapter suggests checking whether a very thick layer of dough still gives a thin side to the puri. Sana in Jabalpur wants to test this by frying a thin dough circle and a very thick one. Write her plan: (a) the one thing she will change; (b) two things she will keep the same; (c) what she will observe for each puri; (d) one more thing she should note down while frying.
questions.a: (a) The thickness of the dough circle (thin and very thick). (b) Any two of: the same flour, the same oil temperature, the same way of putting the dough into the oil, the same size of circle. (c) Whether one side of the puri comes out thinner than the other (yes/no). (d) Anything else she sees or senses, for example whether the oil splattered, smelled or smoked.
s: (a) Changes only the thickness
(b) Two conditions kept the same
(c) Observes whether one side is thinner
(d) Notes something else seen or sensed, such as splatter, smell or smoke

questions.q: Rhea uses the same atta, hot oil and the same way of sliding the dough in for every puri. Her 3 mm puris took 5 s, 4 s and 6 s to puff, and her 6 mm puris took 9 s, 8 s and 10 s. Which conclusion do her trials support best?
questions.a: In these trials, the thicker circles took longer to puff up.
o: In these trials, the thicker circles took longer to puff up.
In these trials, the thicker circles did not puff up at all.
In these trials, the oil temperature made the thicker circles slower.
In these trials, thickness made no difference to the time taken.

questions.q: After one round of puri trials, Arav's notes end with: 'All today's dough was made fresh this morning. I wonder whether dough kept in the fridge overnight would behave differently.' (a) Write the new question his notes raise, as a question he could investigate. (b) In his next round, what one thing should he change, and name one thing he should keep the same?
questions.a: (a) Do puris puff better when made from fresh dough or from stored (overnight) dough? (b) Change only whether the dough is fresh or stored; keep, for example, the same thickness, the same oil temperature or the same way of putting the dough into the oil.
s: (a) States the fresh-versus-stored dough question
(b) Changes only fresh/stored and names one condition kept the same

questions.q: Tina has little time, so she says, 'I will change the oil temperature and the type of flour together in my next puri. If it puffs faster, I will know which change made it faster.' Check her claim using the chapter, and suggest a better plan.
questions.a: She is wrong. If two things are changed at once, a faster puff could be due to either the oil or the flour, so she cannot tell which change made the difference. The chapter says it is better to change only one thing at a time while keeping the other conditions the same, so she should first change only the oil temperature (keeping the flour the same), and test the flour in a separate set of trials.
s: Says the claim is wrong
Explains that with two changes the cause cannot be told apart
Better plan: change one thing at a time, keeping the rest the same

questions.q: A group in Bhubaneswar records three puris, all rolled to 4 mm from the same atta. Puri A: hot oil, dropped vertically, puffed in 6 s. Puri B: boiling hot oil, slid in slowly, puffed in 3 s. Puri C: not very hot oil, dropped vertically, puffed in 11 s. They conclude, 'Hotter oil makes a puri puff faster.' Which comparison in their record is fair, which is not, and how far does their record support the conclusion?
questions.a: A and C are a fair comparison: only the oil temperature differs (hot against not very hot), and the hotter oil puffed sooner (6 s against 11 s). B cannot be fairly compared with A or C, because both the oil temperature and the way the dough went in were changed. So the record supports 'hot oil puffed faster than not very hot oil' from A and C only; it does not show anything about boiling hot oil until a boiling-hot puri is dropped vertically like A and C.
s: Identifies A and C as fair (only oil changed), 6 s against 11 s
Says B changed two things, so it is not a fair comparison
Limits the conclusion to hot against not very hot oil

questions.q:
A tiffin centre in Hyderabad needs 120 well-puffed puris for a school's breakfast. The cook tests the chapter's question about fresh and stored dough: 10 puris from dough made fresh in the morning and 10 from dough made the night before. Of the fresh-dough puris, 9 puffed; of the stored-dough puris, 6 puffed. Each dough circle costs Rs 2. Using fresh dough means the cook must come one hour earlier, for which he is paid Rs 100 extra.
(a) Name two conditions the cook must keep the same for this to be a fair test.
(b) What percentage of each kind puffed?
(c) At these rates, how many dough circles of each kind are needed to get 120 puffed puris?
(d) Which dough should the centre use? Justify with the total cost, and say one reason to be careful with this decision.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: the same thickness and size of circle, the same flour, the same oil temperature, the same way of putting the dough into the oil. (b) Fresh: 9 of 10 = 90%. Stored: 6 of 10 = 60%. (c) Fresh: 120 / 0.9 = 133.3, so 134 circles. Stored: 120 / 0.6 = 200 circles. (d) Fresh dough: 134 x Rs 2 + Rs 100 = Rs 368. Stored dough: 200 x Rs 2 = Rs 400. Fresh dough is cheaper by Rs 32, so the centre should use fresh dough. Be careful, because only 10 puris of each kind were tested; a larger round of trials would make the decision more reliable.
s: (a) Two conditions kept the same
(b) 90% fresh and 60% stored
(c) 134 fresh circles and 200 stored circles
(d) Rs 368 against Rs 400, chooses fresh dough and notes the small number of trials

questions.q:
Rahul investigates the chapter's question 'What happens if I prick a hole in the puri before frying?'. His record:
Trial 1: no hole, 4 mm, hot oil, slid at an angle - puffed, 5 s
Trial 2: one hole, 4 mm, hot oil, slid at an angle - did not puff
Trial 3: one hole, 6 mm, boiling hot oil, dropped vertically - puffed a little, 7 s
Trial 4: no hole, 4 mm, hot oil, slid at an angle - puffed, 6 s
He wrote down nothing else. His conclusion: 'A hole stops a puri from puffing, but thicker dough in hotter oil can beat the hole.'
(a) Which trials make a fair comparison of 'hole' against 'no hole'?
(b) Why can Trial 3 not test the second half of his conclusion?
(c) Name one yes/no observation and one number observation in his record.
(d) Which habit of a systematic investigation did he skip by writing nothing else?
(e) Evaluate his conclusion and suggest the next trial he should do.
questions.a: (a) Trials 1, 2 and 4: only the hole differs; thickness (4 mm), oil (hot) and the way of putting the dough in (slid at an angle) are the same. (b) Compared with Trial 2, Trial 3 changed three things at once (thickness, oil temperature and the way the dough went in), so any difference cannot be put down to one of them. (c) Yes/no: whether the puri puffed. Number: the time to puff, in seconds. (d) Keeping notes of everything seen and sensed, such as whether the oil splattered, smelled or smoked. (e) The first half is supported by Trials 1, 2 and 4 (only the pricked puri failed to puff). The second half is not supported, because Trial 3 was not a fair test. Next trial: one hole, 6 mm, hot oil, slid at an angle, changing only the thickness compared with Trial 2.
s: (a) Trials 1, 2 and 4, with only the hole differing
(b) Trial 3 changed thickness, oil and way of dropping at once
(c) Puffed yes/no and time in seconds
(d) Keeping notes of everything seen and sensed
(e) First half supported, second half not; next trial changes only thickness
